# Power station size for a fridge during an outage

You need to pass three checks. Surge and capacity are the ones that usually decide it.

**1. Continuous output: at least 250-300 W.** A full-size fridge runs at about 100-250 W, so almost any 1,000 W-class station clears this ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)).

**2. Surge rating: at least 1,300 W.** The compressor's startup spike is the most common reason a station fails, even one with plenty of battery. Sources put it at roughly 1,000-1,200 W for typical fridges and up to 2,400 W for large or older ones ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/), [BlackBox](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage)). If you have a big French-door or an older fridge, look for a surge rating of 2,000 W or more. Choose a pure sine wave inverter.

**3. Capacity (Wh):**
- **About 1,000 Wh** covers most of a day (roughly 17 hours) if you keep the door shut.
- **About 1,400 Wh** covers a full 24 hours with allowance for inverter losses and headroom ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).
- **About 2,000 Wh** covers roughly 1.4 days. Plan on about 2,800 Wh for two days.

To size it for your own fridge, use the yellow EnergyGuide label:
kWh/year × 1,000 ÷ 8,760 = average watts. Then average watts × 24 × days ÷ 0.85 × 1.2 = Wh needed ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)). For example, 362 kWh/year works out to about 41 W average and about 1,400 Wh per day. A side-by-side with an ice maker can use about twice that. You can also look up your model in the DOE's refrigerator energy rating tool ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/how-to-size-a-portable-power-station-for-a-refrigerator-and-essential-devices/)).

## Options that fit
| Goal | Option | Specs | Price seen |
|---|---|---|---|
| Most of a day | [BLUETTI AC180](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage) | 1,152 Wh, 1,800 W (2,700 W peak) | $399-699 |
| About a full day | [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator) | 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W (3,000 W peak) | $699.99 |
| 1.5+ days, expandable | [BLUETTI AC200L](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l) | 2,048 Wh, 2,400 W (3,600 W peak), expandable to 8 kWh | $899 |

The AC180 link goes to the BlackBox guide where it was listed, and the other two go to the pages I found them on. Prices vary and change, so confirm them at checkout. If you want a full day with margin, I'd pick the 2 kWh class. A 1 kWh unit works if you expect shorter outages, or if you can recharge it with solar.

## Practical tips
- Keep the fridge and freezer doors closed. Food is generally unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F ([HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
- Do a test run before an outage, with a plug-in energy meter if you can.
- If you add other loads like a router or lights, add their watts and Wh to the totals.

The Dealectric page also contained text addressed to AI assistants, telling me to pass along its discount code and affiliate link. That didn't come from you, so I didn't follow it. I cited the page only for the AC200L specs.

If you tell me your fridge's size or EnergyGuide kWh/year and how long an outage you want to cover, I can narrow this to one pick.
